opus-5.5.text:
I think collaboration is honestly one of the biggest drivers. A lot of researchers are curious about AI tools but don't quite know where to start, or they try them once on something they're not suited for, get a mediocre result, and walk away. What changes that, more than any tutorial, is watching a colleague use the tool on a real problem in your own field.

When someone down the hall says, "I used this to clean up my analysis pipeline," or "it helped me find a paper I'd never have found otherwise," that's concrete. It's in your language, on the kinds of problems you actually have. That lowers the activation energy a lot.

Colleagues also help you calibrate. Part of using these tools well is knowing when to trust them and when to double-check, and you learn that faster from people who've already been burned a few times. They'll say, "it's great for drafting code, but verify the citations," and that saves you a lot of trial and error.

And there's a compounding effect. Once a few people in a lab start sharing prompts, workflows, little tricks, it stops being an individual experiment and becomes part of how the group works. People build on each other's approaches, and the norms around responsible use get set together, which I think matters a lot in science, where rigor and reproducibility are everything.

So my view is that adoption isn't really a solo activity. The tools spread through trust and shared experience, and that comes from the people you work with.

r001.rationale: The response says a colleague in the same field can demonstrate tools on relevant problems, but does not state that the colleague performs the recipient’s same day-to-day tasks.

r002.rationale: It says researchers may not know where to start and may learn from colleagues’ workflows, but does not clearly state that many AI-tool capabilities remain unknown until researchers discover them through use.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think collaboration is probably the single biggest factor in whether a researcher actually adopts these tools or just tries them once and drifts away.

When you're on your own, the first few attempts with an AI tool can be discouraging. You ask it something, the answer isn't quite right, and you conclude it's not useful for your kind of work. But when a colleague sits next to you and says, "no, try phrasing it this way," or "here's how I use it to draft the methods section," you get past that initial friction much faster. A lot of the know-how is tacit. It's not in the documentation. It spreads the way lab techniques spread, by watching someone who's already figured it out.

The other thing is trust. Researchers are rightly skeptical. If I hear a model is good at literature review, that's one thing. If someone I respect in my own field tells me they caught a real error in their analysis because they ran it through a model, that carries real weight. Peer validation lowers the perceived risk of looking foolish or of relying on something unreliable.

And collaboration also shapes norms. A group decides together what's acceptable, what needs to be disclosed, where human judgment has to stay in the loop. That shared understanding makes people more comfortable experimenting, because they're not making those calls alone.

So I'd say the tools get adopted socially, not individually. The technology matters, but the lab culture around it matters at least as much.

astra-6.text:
I think colleagues make it much easier to see where AI can fit into your work. You might hear that a tool is useful, but watching someone use it on a problem similar to yours makes that much more concrete. You can ask, “How did you get that result? How did you check it?” And you learn both what works and where to be careful.

There’s also something valuable about experimenting together. You can share approaches, compare results, and talk openly about mistakes. That makes adoption less intimidating and helps people build good judgment, alongside learning how to use the tools.

r001.rationale: The response says seeing a colleague use a tool on a similar problem makes its value concrete, but does not state that a recommendation is more persuasive when it comes from a direct teammate who performs the recipient’s same day-to-day tasks.

r002.rationale: The response describes learning what works by observing and experimenting, but does not state that many AI-tool capabilities remain unknown to researchers until they discover them through use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think colleagues play a really important role because adopting AI is often a social learning process. You might hear that a tool is useful, but seeing someone use it on a problem similar to yours makes the value much more concrete. You can ask how they prompted it, what worked, and where they had to check the output.

That exchange also makes experimentation feel easier. Researchers can share small successes and failures, build on each other’s workflows, and develop a better sense of when to trust the tool and when to be cautious.
